lesson:
# Implication and sequence checking

Most concurrent assertions are implications: whenever an antecedent sequence matches, a consequent must follow. Evaluating them on a trace by hand is the best way to understand what a simulator's assertion engine does each cycle, how attempts overlap, and why a property can pass without checking anything. Vacuity is a central concern for both simulation and formal verification, because a vacuous pass looks exactly like a real one in a summary report.

## Overlapping and non-overlapping implication

`a |-> b` is **overlapping** implication: if $a$ holds at a clock tick, $b$ must hold at the same tick. `a |=> b` is **non-overlapping**: $b$ must hold at the next tick, and it means the same as `a |-> ##1 b`. More generally `a |-> ##k b` checks $b$ exactly $k$ ticks after $a$, and `a |-> ##[1:3] b` accepts $b$ at any of the next three ticks. A new attempt of the property starts at every clock tick, so attempts overlap: an antecedent at cycle 3 and another at cycle 4 each create their own obligation. Operand values are the sampled values at each tick, that is, the values just before each clock edge.

## Counting failures on a trace

Evaluate each attempt separately. Take `a |-> ##1 b` over cycles 1 to 8 with $a$ = 1 0 1 1 0 0 1 0 and $b$ = 0 1 0 1 0 1 1 0. Attempts starting in cycles 1 to 7 complete inside the trace. Antecedents hold at cycles 1, 3, 4 and 7. The consequent is checked one cycle later: $b$ at cycle 2 is 1 (pass), at cycle 4 is 1 (pass), at cycle 5 is 0 (fail), at cycle 8 is 0 (fail). So 2 attempts fail. With `a |-> b` instead, the checks are at cycles 1, 3, 4 and 7: $b$ = 0, 0, 1, 1, so the attempts at cycles 1 and 3 fail. A simulator reports each failure at the cycle where the consequent is found false, which may be several cycles after the antecedent.

## Vacuous success

An attempt whose antecedent does not match succeeds **vacuously**: the implication is true because nothing was required. In the trace above, the attempts at cycles 2, 5 and 6 are vacuous, the two at cycles 1 and 3 are real passes and two fail. A property that only ever passes vacuously has checked nothing: `req |-> ##1 ack` on a testbench that never asserts req reports success on every cycle. Simulators can count vacuous and non-vacuous passes separately, and good practice adds `cover property (a)` for each antecedent so coverage proves the check was exercised. In formal verification, vacuity checking asks whether the antecedent can ever occur at all under the constraints, catching over-constrained environments.

## Going deeper

label: UVM architecture
lesson:
# UVM architecture

The Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) is a SystemVerilog class library and a set of conventions for building reusable testbenches. Its value is structural: a standard component hierarchy, standard communication through transaction-level ports, and standard ways to configure and vary it. A tool designer meets UVM as the dominant workload of commercial simulators and as the vocabulary in which verification teams describe their environments.

## The component hierarchy

A UVM testbench is a tree of components. At the top is a **test**, which builds an **environment** and decides configuration and stimulus. The environment contains one **agent** per DUT interface, plus a **scoreboard** and coverage collectors. An active agent contains a **sequencer**, which arbitrates and supplies transactions; a **driver**, which turns each transaction into pin activity through a virtual interface; and a **monitor**, which observes the pins and publishes reconstructed transactions through an analysis port. Monitors feed the scoreboard and coverage, so checking sees exactly what happened on the pins. Every component knows only its own job and talks to others through ports, which is what lets components be swapped and reused.

## Active and passive agents and reuse

An agent can be **active**, with sequencer and driver creating traffic, or **passive**, with only a monitor. At block level, the agent for a bus interface is active: the testbench drives the DUT. At SoC level, the same interface may be driven by another block of real RTL; the agent is reconfigured as passive, and its monitor, protocol checks and coverage keep working unchanged. This vertical reuse is a central goal of the methodology: protocol knowledge is written once in an agent and carried from block to subsystem to chip. Coordinated traffic across several agents is produced by virtual sequences that start sequences on each agent's sequencer, rather than by wiring drivers together.

## Components versus objects

UVM separates **components** (derived from `uvm_component`) from **objects** (derived from `uvm_object`). Components form the static hierarchy: drivers, monitors, agents, environments, scoreboards. They are created during the build phase at time 0, have a place in the tree and a hierarchical name, and take part in phasing. Objects are transient data: transactions (`uvm_sequence_item`), sequences, configuration objects. They are created, randomized, passed around and discarded many times during a run. A component created late, for example with `new()` in the middle of the run phase, misses the build and connect phases and is never configured or connected. Keeping this distinction clear is what makes the hierarchy predictable.

## Going deeper

Accellera, "Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) 1.2 User's Guide" (2015); IEEE Std 1800.2-2020 (UVM class reference); Salemi, "The UVM Primer" (2013).

lesson:
# UVM phasing and objections

A UVM testbench is a program with many cooperating components, and they must be built, connected, run and shut down in a coordinated order. UVM phasing is that order. It also defines when the test ends, through objections. Most UVM failures that look like "the test did nothing" or "the test never ends" are phasing errors, and the traversal rules are a small application of tree traversal over the component hierarchy.

## The phase sequence and traversal order

The common phases are, in order: **build**, **connect**, **end_of_elaboration**, **start_of_simulation**, **run**, **extract**, **check**, **report** and **final**. All except run are functions that take no simulation time. Build executes **top-down**: a parent's build_phase runs before its children's, because the parent creates and configures its children there, a pre-order traversal of the tree. Connect and the later function phases execute **bottom-up**, like a post-order traversal; by then the whole tree exists, so every port a component connects is already built. The run phase is a task, started in parallel in every component, and it is the only common phase that consumes simulation time.

## Run-time phases and objections

The run phase ends when no component holds an **objection**. A test raises an objection before starting its main sequence and drops it when the sequence completes; drivers and scoreboards may also object while work is pending. When the count of raised objections reaches zero, after any configured drain time, run ends and the cleanup phases follow. If no objection is ever raised, the run phase ends at time 0 and the test finishes before its sequence does anything. If an objection is never dropped, the test hangs until a timeout. In parallel with run_phase, UVM also schedules run-time sub-phases (reset, configure, main, shutdown and their pre and post variants), each ending by the same objection mechanism.

## Using the phases correctly

Each kind of work has a phase. Read configuration with `uvm_config_db::get` in build_phase, before creating or configuring children. Create components only in build_phase, never in connect or run. Make port connections in connect_phase. Do final checks, such as reporting expected transactions that never arrived, in check_phase, after all traffic has ended. Report summaries in report_phase. Because function phases cannot block, setup is guaranteed to complete before simulation time advances. The phase schedule is also where a simulator's performance shows: build of a large hierarchy can take noticeable time, and the run phase is where the DUT and the testbench actually compete for CPU.

## Going deeper

Accellera, "UVM 1.2 User's Guide" (2015), chapter on phasing; IEEE Std 1800.2-2020, the uvm_phase and uvm_objection classes.

label: Sequences, sequencers and drivers
lesson:
# Sequences, sequencers and drivers

UVM separates what traffic to generate from how to put it on the pins. Sequences describe scenarios as streams of randomized transactions; drivers implement the protocol. The two meet through a sequencer and a precise handshake. Understanding that handshake, arbitration among sequences, and virtual sequences explains how one environment supports hundreds of tests without changing a line of driver code.

## The sequence, sequencer and driver handshake

A sequence's `body()` task produces items. For each item it calls `start_item(req)`, which blocks until the sequencer grants it access to the driver; it randomizes the item; then `finish_item(req)` hands the item over and blocks until the driver is done. On the other side, the driver loops on `seq_item_port.get_next_item(req)`, drives the item onto the interface over as many cycles as the protocol needs, and calls `seq_item_port.item_done()`, which releases the sequence. Randomizing between start_item and finish_item is **late randomization**: constraints can depend on the state at the moment the driver is ready. If a driver never calls item_done, the sequence blocks in finish_item forever.

## Arbitration, responses and virtual sequences

Several sequences can run on one sequencer at once, for example background traffic plus an error-injection sequence. The sequencer arbitrates among their start_item requests according to its arbitration mode, such as FIFO order, priority or random. A sequence that needs uninterrupted access for a multi-item operation takes `lock()` or `grab()`. Responses travel back the same way: the driver returns a response item and the sequence retrieves it with `get_response`. A **virtual sequence** generates no items itself; it starts sequences on several agents' sequencers in a coordinated order, for example configuring registers through one interface and then starting data traffic on two others. Virtual sequences are where multi-interface scenarios live.

## Layering and reuse

Keeping stimulus in sequences means tests vary traffic without editing the environment: a test selects which sequence to start, sets a default sequence for a sequencer, or uses a factory override to replace the item type with a derived class carrying extra constraints. Sequences can be **layered**: a packet-level sequence produces packets, and a translation layer converts each packet into the byte-level items a lower sequencer and driver understand, so each layer randomizes and collects coverage at its own abstraction. Libraries of sequences, chosen at random in regression, mix scenarios in random order so their interactions are exercised. The driver stays small, protocol-only and stable, which also makes it the right place for protocol assertions.

label: The UVM factory and configuration database
lesson:
# The UVM factory and configuration database

A reusable environment must let each test change behavior without editing shared code. UVM provides two mechanisms for this. The **factory** substitutes derived classes for base classes at creation time. The **configuration database** passes values and handles, including virtual interfaces, down the hierarchy by path. Both are lookups resolved at run time, so they are flexible, and their failure modes are silent unless code checks for them.

## Factory creation and overrides

Components and objects registered with the factory (through the `uvm_component_utils` or `uvm_object_utils` macros) are created with `my_driver::type_id::create("drv", this)` rather than `new()`. The factory checks its override table first. A **type override**, such as `set_type_override_by_type(base_item::get_type(), err_item::get_type())`, makes every factory creation of `base_item` return an `err_item`, a derived class that might add error-injection constraints. An **instance override** applies only at matching hierarchical paths, for example to the driver of one agent out of two. Anything built with `new()` bypasses the factory, so overrides silently fail to apply to it, which is the most common factory bug.

## The configuration database

`uvm_config_db#(T)::set(context, "path", "field", value)` stores a value for components whose hierarchical names match the path, which can contain wildcards. A component retrieves it with `uvm_config_db#(T)::get(this, "", "field", var)`, normally in build_phase. The typical use is passing a virtual interface from the top-level module, which instantiates the real interface, into the driver and monitor, which are classes and cannot reach module instances directly. Precedence matters: during build, a set made from higher in the hierarchy wins over one made lower, so a test can override an environment's defaults. After build, the last set wins. Configuration objects bundle many fields into one class to keep this manageable.

## Silent failures and defensive use

Both mechanisms resolve strings at run time, so mistakes do not fail compilation. A path typo, such as setting "env.agnt*" for a component named "env.agent0", matches nothing; the get returns 0, leaves the variable unchanged, and the component runs with its default. A get that runs before the corresponding set, because of phase ordering, has the same effect. Defensive code checks the return value of every get and reports a fatal error for required items such as virtual interfaces, and tests print the factory's override table and the config_db's contents in debug runs. Changing configuration during the run phase invites races between set and get and is best avoided: configuration shapes construction and belongs in build.

## Going deeper

Accellera, "UVM 1.2 User's Guide" (2015), chapters on the factory and the configuration database; IEEE Std 1800.2-2020, uvm_factory and uvm_config_db.

label: Transaction-level modeling and TLM ports
lesson:
# Transaction-level modeling and TLM ports

Transaction-level modeling (TLM) describes communication as function calls that carry whole transactions, not as signal changes on pins. Inside a UVM testbench, TLM ports connect components. In SystemC, TLM-2.0 is the standard for building fast virtual platforms of processors, buses and peripherals. Both rest on the same idea: abstracting time and pins away makes simulation orders of magnitude faster, at a cost in timing accuracy that has to be managed explicitly.

## Ports, exports and analysis ports

A TLM **port** is where a component calls an interface method such as `put`, `get` or `write`; an **export** forwards the interface through a hierarchy level; an **imp** (implementation) is where the method is actually implemented. Connecting port to imp means the caller invokes the callee's method directly. Put and get can block, so they suit producer-consumer pairs, often decoupled by a `uvm_tlm_fifo`. The **analysis port** is special: its `write` method is a function, so it takes zero simulation time and never blocks, and it broadcasts each transaction to every connected subscriber, one call per subscriber. With zero subscribers the write is still legal and simply goes nowhere. That is why monitors publish through analysis ports: a monitor never waits on, or even knows about, its consumers.

## SystemC TLM-2.0: loosely and approximately timed

TLM-2.0 defines a **generic payload** (command, address, data pointer, length, byte enables, response status) and two transport styles. **Loosely timed** models use `b_transport`, a blocking call that completes the whole transaction and returns with a timing annotation: the target adds its delay to a time argument instead of waiting. This is fast and is the basis of virtual platforms that boot software before RTL exists. **Approximately timed** models use `nb_transport` calls with explicit phases (BEGIN_REQ, END_REQ, BEGIN_RESP, END_RESP), so pipelining, outstanding transactions and contention can be modeled. Neither style is cycle-accurate; checking an arbiter's cycle-level fairness needs RTL. A scoreboard comparing a TLM reference model against RTL must compare transaction content and order, not cycle timing.

## Temporal decoupling and the quantum

A loosely timed initiator does not need to synchronize with the SystemC kernel on every transaction. With **temporal decoupling**, it keeps a local time offset and runs ahead of global simulation time, yielding to the kernel only when the offset reaches the **global quantum**. Over $T$ of simulated time with quantum $q$, it synchronizes about $T/q$ times. Example: with $q = 500$ ns over 100 us of simulated time, it synchronizes 200 times instead of once per transaction. Raising the quantum to 5 us cuts synchronizations by a factor of 10 and speeds simulation, because context switches into the kernel are expensive. The price is accuracy: initiators can disagree about time by up to one quantum, so interactions between them, such as a shared flag polled by two processors, become less precise.

## Going deeper

IEEE Std 1666-2011 (SystemC, including TLM-2.0); Accellera, "UVM 1.2 User's Guide" (2015), chapter on TLM; Aynsley, "OSCI TLM-2.0 Language Reference Manual" (2009).

label: CDC verification and synchronizers
lesson:
# CDC verification and synchronizers

Whenever a signal crosses from one clock domain to an unrelated one, the receiving flop can sample it while it changes and go metastable. Clock-domain crossing (CDC) verification checks that every such crossing uses a correct synchronization scheme. It sits between simulation and static analysis, because ordinary RTL simulation is blind to the failure: it never models metastability. A verification tool designer needs both the circuit facts and the reasons simulation misses them.

## Metastability and the two-flop synchronizer

If a flop's data input changes inside its setup-hold window, the flop can enter a metastable state and take an unbounded, though usually short, time to resolve to 0 or 1. Across asynchronous clocks this will happen eventually, so it cannot be prevented, only made harmless. The standard **two-flop synchronizer** feeds the asynchronous signal into a flop clocked by the destination clock, then into a second flop. The first flop may go metastable; it has almost a full destination clock period to resolve before the second flop samples it, so the probability that metastability propagates beyond the second flop is tiny. The synchronizer does not fix the latency: the destination sees a change one cycle earlier or later depending on when it was sampled, and designs must tolerate that.

## Structural CDC checks

Static CDC tools find every path between domains and classify the scheme used. Common violations: **combinational logic before the synchronizer**, whose glitches can be captured as false pulses, so a crossing must start from a flop; **fanout of the first synchronizer stage** to several loads, which can resolve differently; **reconvergence**, where related bits pass through separate synchronizers and recombine, arriving in different cycles and forming combinations the source never produced; and **fast-to-slow pulses**, where a one-cycle pulse in a fast domain can fall between slow-domain edges and vanish, requiring pulse stretching, a toggle scheme or a handshake. Multi-bit values need Gray coding, a handshake that holds data stable, or an asynchronous FIFO. The tool reports each crossing as synchronized, unsynchronized or using a recognized scheme.

## Why simulation misses CDC bugs

In zero-delay RTL simulation, a flop always captures a clean value, and the synchronizer's latency is always exactly two cycles. Metastability never happens, and the one-cycle uncertainty never appears, so logic that only works with one particular latency passes every test. This is why CDC is checked structurally and with formal protocol checks, and why simulation adds **metastability injection**: a model that randomly adds or removes one cycle of delay at each synchronizer output, emulating unpredictable resolution. Under injection, reconvergence bugs and fragile handshakes show up as test failures. Assertions on handshake signals, such as "data is stable while the request is pending", catch protocol errors that structure alone cannot see: a structurally correct crossing can still be used incorrectly.

## Going deeper

Ginosar, "Metastability and synchronizers: a tutorial", IEEE Design and Test of Computers (2011); Cummings, "Clock Domain Crossing (CDC) Design and Verification Techniques Using SystemVerilog" (SNUG 2008).

label: Synchronizer MTBF
lesson:
# Synchronizer MTBF

A synchronizer cannot eliminate metastability, so its quality is a failure rate. The mean time between failures (MTBF) model turns flop parameters, clock rates and the time allowed for resolution into a number of seconds or years. Because the resolution time enters an exponential, small design changes move MTBF by many orders of magnitude, which is why synchronizer design is a quantitative engineering decision rather than a rule of thumb.

## The MTBF formula

A flop that samples an asynchronous input goes metastable at a rate proportional to how often the input changes and how often it is sampled: $T_0 f_{clk} f_{data}$ events per second, where $T_0$ is a window parameter of the flop (in seconds), $f_{clk}$ the sampling clock frequency and $f_{data}$ the data toggle rate. A metastable flop resolves exponentially: the probability that it is still unresolved after time $t$ is about $e^{-t/\tau}$, where $\tau$ is the resolution time constant of the flop, a few to tens of picoseconds in modern processes. A failure happens when metastability lasts longer than the available resolution time $t_r$. So
$$\text{MTBF} = \frac{e^{t_r/\tau}}{T_0 \, f_{clk} \, f_{data}}.$$
Both $T_0$ and $\tau$ are characterized per flop and per process corner.

## Computing MTBF

Take $\tau = 20$ ps, $T_0 = 50$ ps, $f_{clk} = 500$ MHz, $f_{data} = 50$ MHz and $t_r = 400$ ps. The denominator is $50 \times 10^{-12} \cdot 5 \times 10^8 \cdot 5 \times 10^7 = 1.25 \times 10^6$ per second. The exponent is $400/20 = 20$, and $e^{20} \approx 4.85 \times 10^8$. So MTBF $\approx 4.85 \times 10^8 / 1.25 \times 10^6 \approx 388$ seconds: a failure every six and a half minutes, useless. Now allow nearly a full 2 ns clock period for resolution, $t_r = 1800$ ps: the exponent is 90 and MTBF is about $10^{33}$ seconds. The answer depends almost entirely on $t_r/\tau$; the frequencies matter only linearly.

## Adding stages and designing to a target

Adding a third synchronizer flop gives roughly one more destination clock period $T$ of resolution time, multiplying MTBF by $e^{T/\tau}$. At 1 GHz with $\tau = 20$ ps that factor is $e^{50}$, about $10^{21.7}$: almost 22 orders of magnitude. Conversely, the resolution time needed for a target MTBF is $t_r = \tau \ln(\text{MTBF} \cdot T_0 f_{clk} f_{data})$, and every extra factor of 10 in MTBF costs only $\tau \ln 10 \approx 2.3\tau$ of time. A chip contains many synchronizers, and the system failure rate is their sum, so a product with 1,000 synchronizers needs each to be 1,000 times better than the system target. High clock rates, slow corners (larger $\tau$) and logic between the synchronizer flops all shrink $t_r$ and must be included.

## Going deeper

Ginosar, "Metastability and synchronizers: a tutorial", IEEE Design and Test of Computers (2011); Kleeman and Cantoni, "Metastable behavior in digital systems", IEEE Design and Test of Computers (1987).

Round to 1 decimal place.

lesson:
# Multi-bit crossings, Gray codes and async FIFOs

A two-flop synchronizer makes one bit safe. A multi-bit value is not made safe by synchronizing every bit, because the bits resolve independently and can be captured from different cycles. Gray codes, handshakes and asynchronous FIFOs are the standard answers. Their arithmetic (how many bits change, what code to use, how deep a FIFO must be) is a routine part of CDC design and verification.

## Why multi-bit binary crossings fail

Suppose a 4-bit binary counter crosses domains with a synchronizer on each bit, and it increments from 7 (0111) to 8 (1000). All four bits change at once. The destination samples each bit near the transition, and each synchronizer may capture the old or the new value independently, so the destination can see any of 16 values, such as 1111 or 0000, neither of which the source ever held. In general, going from $k$ to $k + 1$ changes the trailing ones of $k$ plus one more bit: $\text{popcount}(k \oplus (k+1))$ bits. Only when exactly one bit changes per transition is every possible sample either the old value or the new one. That is the property a Gray code provides.

## Gray codes

The reflected binary Gray code of $b$ is $g = b \oplus (b \gg 1)$. Consecutive integers have Gray codes that differ in exactly one bit, including the wrap from the maximum back to 0. Example: $b = 13 = 1101_2$, $b \gg 1 = 0110_2$, so $g = 1011_2 = 11$. And $14 = 1110_2$ gives $1110 \oplus 0111 = 1001_2 = 9$; 1011 and 1001 differ in one bit. Decoding back to binary takes a prefix XOR: each binary bit is the XOR of all Gray bits at or above it. Gray coding only works for values that change by one step at a time, such as counters and FIFO pointers; arbitrary data words need a handshake that holds the data stable while a single synchronized control bit announces it.

## Asynchronous FIFOs and their depth

An asynchronous FIFO moves a stream of data words between domains. Its write and read pointers are kept in binary for addressing, converted to Gray code, and synchronized into the opposite domain, where they are compared to produce full and empty flags. The data itself sits in a dual-port memory and needs no synchronization, because the flags guarantee it is stable when read. Sizing: a burst of $B$ words written at $f_w$ while the reader drains at $f_r < f_w$ leaves a backlog of $B(1 - f_r/f_w)$ words at the end of the burst. For $B = 80$, $f_w = 200$ MHz and $f_r = 125$ MHz, that is $80 \times 0.375 = 30$ words, so at least 30 entries, plus margin for the few cycles of synchronizer latency on the pointers, which makes the flags conservative.

## Going deeper

Cummings, "Simulation and Synthesis Techniques for Asynchronous FIFO Design" (SNUG 2002); Ginosar, "Metastability and synchronizers: a tutorial", IEEE Design and Test of Computers (2011).

lesson:
# Reset synchronizers and reset-domain crossing

Resets cross domains too. An asynchronous reset asserts without a clock, which is useful, but its release is a timing event relative to each flop's clock, and an asynchronous reset in one part of a design can corrupt flops elsewhere that are not reset. Reset synchronizers handle the first problem; reset-domain crossing (RDC) analysis handles the second. Both are invisible to zero-delay RTL simulation, which is why they need dedicated checks.

## Reset synchronizers

A flop with an asynchronous reset has **recovery** and **removal** requirements: the reset must be released some time before the clock edge (recovery) and not too soon after it (removal), the reset-pin equivalents of setup and hold. If an external reset is released at an arbitrary time, some flops may leave reset one cycle earlier than others, or go metastable. A **reset synchronizer** fixes this: two flops clocked by the local clock, both asynchronously reset by the external reset, with the first flop's data input tied to the inactive level. Reset asserts immediately and asynchronously, through the flops' reset pins, and deasserts synchronously, rippling through the two flops on clock edges. Each clock domain needs its own synchronizer, because release must be synchronous to that domain's clock.

## Reset-domain crossings

A **reset-domain crossing** is a path from a flop reset by one reset to a flop reset by a different reset, or not reset at all, even when both are on the same clock. When the source's reset asserts, its output changes immediately, at a time unrelated to the destination clock. If the destination keeps capturing, it can sample that change inside its setup-hold window and go metastable, or capture a value the protocol never allowed. Typical cases are soft resets of one block while the rest of the chip runs, and power or debug resets. The standard fixes are to isolate the destination during the source reset, for example by holding its enable or clock-gating it, or to order the resets so the destination is reset first. Static timing analysis does not normally time these asynchronous paths against the destination clock, so dedicated RDC tools check them structurally.

## Verifying reset behavior

Reset bugs escape simulation in specific ways. Zero-delay simulation releases reset cleanly at one instant, so recovery and removal problems never appear. Two-state simulation starts every flop at a defined value, hiding flops that lack a reset. Four-state simulation helps with the second: flops that are not reset start at X, and X-propagation shows logic that depends on them before initialization, as long as X-optimistic constructs do not mask it. Verification of resets therefore combines four-state reset tests, structural reset and RDC checks, assertions on reset ordering (for example that one domain leaves reset only after another), and gate-level simulation with timing for the release sequence of critical blocks. Partial and soft resets need special scenarios: reset one block while traffic runs elsewhere and check that nothing outside is corrupted.

## Going deeper

Cummings, Mills and Golson, "Asynchronous and Synchronous Reset Design Techniques, Part Deux" (SNUG 2003); Ginosar, "Metastability and synchronizers: a tutorial", IEEE Design and Test of Computers (2011).

lesson:
# Emulation and FPGA prototyping

Software simulation of a full SoC runs far too slowly to boot an operating system or run real workloads. Hardware-assisted verification runs the design on hardware instead: **emulators** built from custom processors or FPGAs, and **FPGA prototypes**. They change what verification can reach, from millions of cycles to billions, and they impose their own constraints on the design, the testbench and debugging.

## Emulators and prototypes

An **emulator** compiles the synthesizable design onto dedicated hardware, either arrays of special-purpose processors that evaluate logic in parallel or large arrays of FPGAs, and runs it orders of magnitude faster than a software simulator. Emulators are built for verification: they capture signal traces deeply for debug, support fast recompiles after a change, and serve many users from a shared machine. An **FPGA prototype** maps the design onto commercial FPGA boards and runs faster still, closer to real system speed, but with limited visibility into internal signals and longer bring-up, because the design must be partitioned, constrained and timed for the FPGAs. Both require synthesizable RTL: behavioral delays, unsynthesizable testbench code and four-state X semantics have no direct hardware meaning.

## Testbenches and transactors

A conventional testbench runs on a host computer. If the emulated DUT had to exchange signal values with the host on every clock, the link latency would cap its speed near that of simulation. The standard solution is **transaction-based acceleration**, or co-modeling: the pin-level parts of the testbench, the drivers and monitors, are written in synthesizable form as **transactors** that run inside the emulator, and only transactions cross the link to the host-side testbench, in batches. The host still runs sequences, scoreboards and coverage, so the verification environment is largely reused. **Speed bridges** connect real external devices, such as a network or memory interface running at full speed, to the slower emulated design by buffering and rate-matching their traffic. Debug visibility is limited by trace storage, so captures are triggered and windowed.

## Choosing the platform

Each platform fits a stage. **Simulation** gives instant turnaround and complete visibility, so it is the right tool while RTL changes daily and blocks are being debugged. **Emulation** runs fast enough to boot an operating system and run driver software on the full SoC before tape-out, while still offering hardware-assisted debug, and it accelerates long regressions. **FPGA prototypes** suit firmware and software teams who need many copies of the design running near real speed for weeks. Speed does not replace checking: an emulator running a billion cycles finds nothing unless scoreboards, assertions and coverage judge what happened. Teams therefore carry the simulation environment forward and measure coverage on every platform.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Simulation versus emulation throughput

Verification platforms differ by orders of magnitude in speed, and they also differ in setup cost: an emulator or prototype must be compiled before it runs. Comparing them is a throughput calculation. The numbers decide which tests run where, how long a regression takes, and when a long compile is worth paying. They also explain why simulator speed per cycle, not per gate, is the figure that matters for system-level verification.

## Simulation speed in cycles per second

A software simulator's speed is measured in simulated clock cycles per second of wall time. It falls roughly in proportion to design size and activity, so a large SoC that simulates at a few hundred cycles per second is normal, while a small block may run at hundreds of thousands. Wall time for a test is cycles divided by speed. A 20-million-cycle boot sequence at 500 cycles per second takes $2 \times 10^7 / 500 = 40{,}000$ seconds, about 11.11 hours. A billion-cycle software workload would take more than three weeks. These numbers explain the push toward compiled simulation, parallel simulation and hardware acceleration: system-level scenarios are long, and simulation time is linear in their length.

## Emulation time including compile

An emulator runs much faster, in the range of a megahertz or more for large designs, but each new RTL version must be compiled first, which can take hours. Total time is compile plus run: with a 6-hour compile and a 2 MHz emulation speed, running $50 \times 10^9$ cycles takes $5 \times 10^{10} / 2 \times 10^6 = 25{,}000$ seconds, about 6.94 hours, for a total of 12.94 hours. For short tests, compile dominates; for long ones, run time does. The same compiled image can serve many tests, so the compile cost is shared across a regression, which is why emulation is organized around stable RTL snapshots rather than every edit.

## The break-even test length

Emulation beats simulation for tests longer than a break-even length $N^*$ where the times are equal: $N^*/f_s = C + N^*/f_e$, so $N^* = C / (1/f_s - 1/f_e)$. With $f_s = 200$ cycles per second, $f_e = 1$ MHz and $C = 4$ hours (14,400 s): $1/f_s - 1/f_e = 0.005 - 0.000001 = 0.004999$ s per cycle, so $N^* \approx 2.88$ million cycles. Tests shorter than about 2.9 million cycles finish sooner in simulation, longer ones in emulation. Because $f_e \gg f_s$, the formula is close to $N^* \approx C f_s$: the break-even is the number of cycles the simulator could run during the compile. This is a per-test view; across a regression, shared compiles push the break-even down further.

## Going deeper

Hauck and DeHon (eds.), "Reconfigurable Computing: The Theory and Practice of FPGA-Based Computation" (2008), the chapter on logic emulation; Wile, Goss and Roesner, "Comprehensive Functional Verification" (2005), the chapter on simulation acceleration.

lesson:
# Multi-FPGA partitioning and pin multiplexing

A large SoC does not fit in one FPGA, so emulators and prototypes split it across many. Every net cut by the partition becomes an inter-FPGA signal, and FPGAs have far fewer pins than a large design has cut nets. Time-division multiplexing shares pins among signals at the cost of speed. The resulting system clock is set directly by the cut size, which makes this a graph-partitioning problem with a visible, measurable objective.

## Cut nets become inter-FPGA signals

Model the design as a hypergraph: blocks are vertices and each net is a hyperedge connecting the blocks it touches. Assign each block to an FPGA. A net is **cut** if its blocks sit on more than one FPGA, and each cut net needs a signal between FPGAs. Example: blocks B1, B2, B3 on FPGA A and B4, B5 on FPGA B, with nets {B1, B2}, {B2, B4}, {B3, B5, B1}, {B4, B5} and {B1, B4}. The cut nets are {B2, B4}, {B3, B5, B1} and {B1, B4}: 3 inter-FPGA signals. Moving B4 to FPGA A would cut {B4, B5} instead of {B2, B4} and {B1, B4}, reducing the cut to 2. Partitioners minimize the cut subject to each FPGA's logic capacity, using multilevel methods such as those in hMETIS.

## Time-division multiplexing

Real partitions of large designs cut tens of thousands of signals, while two FPGAs may share only a few hundred pins. **Time-division multiplexing** (TDM) sends several signals over one pin in successive time slots, serializing them at the sender and deserializing at the receiver. The required ratio is $r = \lceil S / P \rceil$ for $S$ cut signals and $P$ available pins. Example: 4,100 signals over 480 pins gives $\lceil 8.54 \rceil = 9$ signals per pin. Ratios differ by link, since each FPGA pair has its own pin budget, and the worst link sets the pace. High-speed serial transceivers raise the per-pin data rate, which allows higher ratios at the same system speed.

## The system clock and why the cut matters

All multiplexed signals must cross before the next system clock edge, so one system cycle needs at least $r$ link cycles, plus overhead for alignment and synchronization. With link clock $f_{link}$, ratio $r$ and $o$ overhead cycles, the system clock is at most $f_{link}/(r + o)$. Example: 500 MHz links, $r = 16$ and 4 overhead cycles give $500/20 = 25$ MHz. Halving the cut halves $r$: with $r = 8$ the clock rises to $500/12 \approx 41.67$ MHz. Paths that cross several FPGAs within one cycle pay this delay more than once. This is a direct line from partition quality to prototype speed, and it is why partitioners for emulation optimize cut size, balance and the number of FPGA hops on timing-critical paths together.

## Going deeper

label: Agentic coverage-closure loops
lesson:
# Agentic coverage-closure loops

Coverage closure is a loop of reading holes, changing stimulus and rerunning, which makes it a natural job for an agent driving the simulator as a tool. The simulator supplies an honest, measurable reward: bins actually hit. The engineering problem is keeping that reward honest, because the cheapest way to raise a coverage number is to change the measurement rather than the stimulus. This concept applies the harness loop, tool-grounded reward and change tiers to closure.

## The closure loop

One iteration reads the merged coverage database at bin level, including cross holes and their hit counts, together with the constraints and sequences that control the relevant fields. The agent proposes a stimulus change: new `dist` weights, a constraint mode, or a new sequence. A cheap pre-check samples the changed constraints with the solver alone, thousands of `randomize()` calls without simulation, to see whether the target values now appear. If they do, the harness runs a regression, merges coverage, and compares against the baseline: which bins were newly hit, whether any were lost, and what the run cost. The result, not the agent's explanation, decides whether the change is kept. This is the edit, build, test loop with coverage as the test.

## Reward design and how it is gamed

A natural reward is the number of newly covered bins. It can be gamed. An agent with write access to the covergroup can add `ignore_bins` for every hole, delete a coverpoint, or lower `option.at_least`, and report 100%. An agent that can touch checkers can weaken a scoreboard comparison so a failing scenario passes and its coverage counts. Stimulus can hit bins in degenerate ways, such as a zero-length burst that technically lands in a "long transfer during flush" cross. Guardrails follow: the coverage model and the checkers are frozen, outside the agent's change surface; reward is measured on a held-out regression; cost (simulation time) is penalized so brute-force seed farming does not win; and sampled traffic for newly hit bins is spot-checked.

## Change tiers for closure

The tiers make the agent's authority explicit. Changing the weight of an existing `dist`, a constraint-mode switch or a plusarg is **Tier 1**, configuration: no new code, trivially reversible. Writing a new sequence class, for example one that throttles the reader so a FIFO fills, is **Tier 2**: new code at a defined extension point, the sequence library, with the environment's core untouched. Editing the DUT, the covergroups, the scoreboard or the reference model is outside the closure agent's remit entirely, and must go to a human, because changing what is measured or what is tested inverts the purpose of verification. Every accepted change ships with its diff, the coverage delta against the baseline and the seeds that reproduce it, so a reviewer can rerun it.

label: LLM-generated testbenches checked by simulation
lesson:
# LLM-generated testbenches checked by simulation

Language models can write testbenches, assertions and reference models quickly. The question is how to trust them. A generated testbench that compiles and passes tells you almost nothing, because a testbench that checks nothing also passes. Simulation supplies the means to measure what matters: does the testbench run, does it reach the intended states, and does it fail when the design is wrong? Mutation testing turns the last question into a number.

## Compile, run and actually check

A harness accepts a generated testbench in stages. First it must compile: errors such as a call to a UVM method that does not exist go straight back to the model as feedback, the cheapest loop. Then it must run to completion on the original RTL without failures. Neither step shows that it checks anything. Common hollow patterns: expected values computed from the DUT's own internal signals, so the DUT is checked against itself; assertions whose antecedents never occur, so every attempt passes vacuously; scoreboards that compare only the first transaction or only a valid flag; stimulus that never leaves reset or never reaches the interesting state. Coverage on the antecedents and on the intended scenarios exposes the reach problems. Checking strength needs a separate measurement.

## Mutation score

**Mutation testing** injects small deliberate bugs (mutants) into the RTL: an operator flipped, a constant changed, a condition inverted. Each mutant is simulated with the testbench; the mutant is **killed** if some test fails. Some mutants are **equivalent**: they do not change observable behavior, so no test can kill them, and they are excluded. The **mutation score** is killed over killable: with 60 mutants, 4 equivalent, and 42 killed, the score is $42 / (60 - 4) = 75\%$. Two testbenches with identical code coverage can have very different scores, because coverage measures what ran and mutation measures what was checked. The original RTL must still pass, otherwise a testbench that always fails would score 100%.

## Failure modes and safe use

A surviving mutant has two common explanations: the tests never exercise the mutated logic (a stimulus gap) or they exercise it but never check the affected output (a checking gap), and both are actionable. Generated reference models deserve the most suspicion. A model produced from the same misreading of the specification as the RTL will agree with it and hide the bug, so a generated model is treated as untrusted until it agrees with an independent source, such as directed cases derived by hand from the specification or an existing golden model. Hallucinated APIs, plausible but wrong protocol timing, and over-constrained stimulus are typical defects. In the harness loop they are caught by compiling, by coverage of intended scenarios, and by mutation score, rather than by reading the code.

C) That the RTL is correct

D) Only that it runs; whether it would detect bugs is still unknown
problems.a: Only that it runs; whether it would detect bugs is still unknown
problems.e: A testbench that never fails gives no evidence; its checking strength must be measured separately.

label: Debug agents and waveform root cause
prereqs: Engines as agent tools over MCP
lesson:
# Debug agents and waveform root cause

When a regression fails, an engineer reproduces it, finds the first wrong value, and traces back to the cause. A debug agent does the same with simulation as its instrument: it reruns, queries waveforms, compares against a reference model, and tests hypotheses by experiment. The simulator makes debugging checkable, since every claim about the root cause can be confirmed by a rerun, and the agent's tool interface decides how efficiently it can ask questions of very large waveform databases.

## Inputs and the first divergence

The agent starts from the failing seed and command line, the scoreboard or assertion message with its time, and the waveform database (VCD, FST or a vendor format). Its first action is to rerun the seed and confirm the failure reproduces deterministically; if it does not, the problem is nondeterminism, a race or an environment issue, and the strategy changes. The scoreboard reports a symptom, often thousands of cycles after the cause: a corrupted pointer at cycle 6,000 may produce wrong data only at cycle 9,000. Root cause is the earliest divergence on the causal path, so the agent compares DUT state, or transactions, against the reference model backwards in time from the symptom.

## Bisection over time and cones

If state matches the reference at cycle 0 and mismatches at cycle $N$, and each rerun from a checkpoint can test whether state still matches at one chosen cycle, bisection finds the first mismatching cycle in $\lceil \log_2 N \rceil$ reruns in the worst case. For $N = 100{,}000$ that is 17 reruns instead of up to 100,000 linear checks. Once the cycle is known, the search moves into space: from the first wrong register, trace its fan-in cone backward to the drivers whose values were wrong at the previous cycle, and repeat until reaching logic whose inputs are right and output is wrong. That logic is the bug's location. Both searches are mechanical, which is what makes them suitable for an agent with good tools.

## Tools, hypotheses and review

Waveform databases are huge, so the agent needs a typed query interface rather than raw text: "values of these signals between these cycles", "first time this signal differs from the reference", "drivers of this net". Exposed as tools, for example over MCP, such queries fit context limits and avoid parsing errors. A proposed root cause is a hypothesis; it is confirmed by experiment: patch or force the suspected logic, rerun the same seed, and check that the mismatch disappears and no new one appears. A failure that vanishes when dumping is turned on points to a race. The output is a report with the reproducing seed, the divergence cycle and location, and the confirming rerun, plus the fix as a diff, because design edits are core changes that a human reviews.

A) To delete the old waveform

B) To get a different random result

C) To confirm the failure reproduces deterministically with the same code and seed

D) To warm up the simulator cache
problems.a: To confirm the failure reproduces deterministically with the same code and seed
problems.e: A non-reproducible failure points to nondeterminism, which changes the debugging strategy.

problems.e: The symptom appears downstream; root cause is the earliest divergence on the causal path.

label: Simulation as a differential test for agent edits
lesson:
# Simulation as a differential test for agent edits

When an agent edits RTL, a testbench or the simulator itself, the change must be shown to do what was intended and nothing else. Simulation provides golden and differential tests: run fixed stimulus with fixed seeds on the old and the new version and compare. The comparison is only as good as its determinism and its stimulus, and the right level of comparison depends on whether timing was supposed to change.

## Golden and differential runs

A **golden test** has fixed inputs, fixed seeds, a recorded simulator version and command line, and recorded expected outputs; it passes only if the outputs are reproduced exactly. A **differential run** applies the same stimulus to two versions, for example the RTL before and after an agent's refactoring, and compares every output cycle by cycle. For a change meant to preserve behavior, any difference is a bug. Determinism is the precondition: a race in the design or testbench makes outputs depend on process order, so differences appear without any real change and drown out true regressions. Races and other nondeterminism must be removed first. Passing a differential run on 50 seeds proves equivalence only on what those seeds exercised; formal equivalence checking covers all inputs.

## What the diff must prove

For an intended change, the proof is the absence of unintended ones: the report must show that only the targeted signals or transactions changed, and everything else matched. When timing is meant to change, such as an added pipeline stage, cycle-by-cycle comparison fails everywhere; compare at transaction level instead, checking content and order. The value system matters. In a four-state simulator, an output that was X after reset in the old version and 0 in the new one is a real difference in initialization, to be explained. A two-state simulator maps X to concrete values, so such differences can vanish, which makes it a weaker oracle for reset and initialization changes. Finally, the differential is only as strong as the stimulus: if the changed module's code coverage is 20%, most of the change was never compared.

## Differential testing across simulators

The same idea applies to the tools. Running one design and testbench on two simulators, such as Icarus Verilog and Verilator, and comparing outputs exposes three kinds of problem: races, where both simulators are compliant but choose different process orders; X-dependent behavior, where four-state and two-state semantics diverge; and genuine simulator bugs. When an agent modifies a simulator, for instance its scheduler for speed, the regression suite must stress exactly the semantics that such changes break: delta-cycle ordering, nonblocking assignments, X propagation, and event controls, compared against the unmodified simulator. Each golden test records the exact simulator version and options, because a legitimate tool change can alter results and would otherwise look like a design regression.

problems.q:
What makes a golden test reliable as a gate for agent edits?

A) A loose tolerance on every output

B) Human inspection of waveforms

C) A new random seed each run

D) Fixed inputs, fixed seeds and recorded expected outputs that are reproduced exactly
problems.a: Fixed inputs, fixed seeds and recorded expected outputs that are reproduced exactly
problems.e: Determinism is what lets a mismatch mean a regression.

problems.q:
What makes a golden test reliable as a gate for agent edits?

A) Fixed inputs, fixed seeds and recorded expected outputs that are reproduced exactly

B) Human inspection of waveforms

C) A loose tolerance on every output

D) A new random seed each run
problems.a: Fixed inputs, fixed seeds and recorded expected outputs that are reproduced exactly
problems.e: Determinism is what lets a mismatch mean a regression.

problems.q:

A) Running only the new RTL's directed tests

B) Checking that it compiles

C) Comparing line counts

D) A differential run: same stimulus and seeds on old and new RTL, with every output compared cycle by cycle
problems.a: A differential run: same stimulus and seeds on old and new RTL, with every output compared cycle by cycle
problems.e: If nothing is supposed to change, any difference in outputs is a bug.

problems.q:

A) It requires more seeds

B) It is slower

C) It cannot compare outputs

D) It maps X to a concrete value, so differences in initialization can vanish
problems.a: It maps X to a concrete value, so differences in initialization can vanish
problems.e: Two-state hides exactly the unknown-state differences that reset changes create.

C) As a real behavioral difference to investigate: the new code initializes something the old did not

D) As equal, because X matches anything
problems.a: As a real behavioral difference to investigate: the new code initializes something the old did not
problems.e: X versus a known value is a difference in initialization, which may or may not be intended.

problems.q:
Why is a two-state simulator weaker than a four-state one as the differential oracle for reset logic?

A) It requires more seeds

B) It cannot compare outputs

C) It is slower

D) It maps X to a concrete value, so differences in initialization can vanish
problems.a: It maps X to a concrete value, so differences in initialization can vanish
problems.e: Two-state hides exactly the unknown-state differences that reset changes create.

problems.q:
An agent modifies a simulator's scheduler for speed. What must the differential test suite include?

A) A single directed test

B) Only synthesizable designs with one clock

C) Only the fastest benchmark

D) Designs with delta-cycle ordering, nonblocking assignments and X behavior, compared against the unmodified simulator
problems.a: Designs with delta-cycle ordering, nonblocking assignments and X behavior, compared against the unmodified simulator
problems.e: Scheduler changes break semantics in subtle orderings, so the tests must stress them.

problems.q:
Running the same RTL and tests in Icarus Verilog and in Verilator gives different outputs. What are the main suspects?

A) Different random seeds always explain it

B) The host operating system

C) A race or X-dependent behavior in the code, or a simulator bug

D) Waveform settings
problems.a: A race or X-dependent behavior in the code, or a simulator bug
problems.e: Cross-simulator differential testing exposes nondeterminism, four-state versus two-state behavior and tool bugs.

problems.q:
A differential check passes but code coverage of the changed module is 20%. What is the conclusion?

A) The check is weak: most of the changed logic was never exercised

B) Coverage does not matter for differential tests

C) The change is proven safe

D) The module is unused
problems.a: The check is weak: most of the changed logic was never exercised
problems.e: Differential testing is only as strong as the stimulus that reaches the change.

label: Seams and change tiers in a simulator
lesson:
# Seams and change tiers in a simulator

A simulator is an engine like a placer or a timer, and the four-layer model applies to it: an immutable core, policies, parameters and observation hooks. Placing each feature in the right layer decides which customer requests are configuration, which are plug-ins, and which would touch the semantics that every result depends on. The seams must also be shaped so that extension does not destroy the compiled speed that makes a modern simulator useful.

## The four layers of a simulator

The **core** is what defines correctness: the scheduling semantics of the language standard (the regions of a time step and their order), the four-state value system and its operator tables, and the event queue's invariants. The **policy** layer holds alternative strategies on top of that core: X-propagation modes (standard semantics versus more pessimistic merging), logic partitioning and ordering heuristics for multithreading, waveform compression schemes. **Parameters** change behavior without code: random seeds, thread counts, optimization levels, plusargs, dump scope. **Observation hooks** let tools read and act on live state: VPI callbacks on value changes and time, coverage and assertion monitors, waveform dumpers. An agent reads state through hooks and changes behavior through parameters and policies.

## Classifying change requests

Requests map onto tiers. Dumping waveforms for one subsystem only is **Tier 1**: a dump-scope setting. A custom X-propagation policy, say one that merges both data inputs of a mux whose select is X, is **Tier 2** if the simulator has an X-propagation seam: a new policy implementing a defined interface, with the value system untouched. A new coverage metric collected during simulation is also Tier 2, a monitor attached at the hooks. Reordering the Active and NBA regions for speed is **Tier 3**, a core edit: it changes language semantics, so it needs human approval and the full regression, and in practice it should be refused. A seam is placed well when the common requests in this list never need Tier 3.

## Designing seams that keep compiled speed

A compiled simulator is fast because the evaluation of the design is straight-line, inlined code. A seam that calls a plug-in on every signal event would destroy that. Seams are therefore coarse: a policy is consulted when code is generated or once per operation type, callbacks fire per cycle or per batch of changes, and plug-ins receive plain data structures. An X-propagation seam needs enough context to decide: the operator, the operand values including their X bits, and where the operation sits (an if condition, a case selector, a mux select). Plug-ins must be deterministic and seedable, with no hidden global state, so that golden and differential tests can tell a regression from noise. A new policy is promoted only after differential runs against the existing simulator on designs that stress ordering and X behavior.

problems.q:
Which of these is a parameter, in the four-layer sense, for a simulator run?

A) The parser for SystemVerilog

B) The VPI callback interface

C) The thread count and the random seed

D) The scheduling regions
problems.a: The thread count and the random seed
problems.e: Parameters change behavior without code: thread count, seeds, plusargs and optimization levels.

problems.q:
Which simulator feature is best treated as a strategy (policy) layer?

A) The X-propagation mode, for example standard LRM semantics versus a more pessimistic merge

B) The order of the NBA region

C) The event queue's correctness invariants

D) The meaning of 1'bx
problems.a: The X-propagation mode, for example standard LRM semantics versus a more pessimistic merge
problems.e: X-handling modes are alternative policies on top of a fixed value system.

problems.q:
Where does an agent read live simulation state, such as signal values or coverage counts, during a run?

A) Through observation hooks such as VPI callbacks and coverage or assertion monitors

B) By editing the scheduler

C) From the compiled C++ source

D) From the synthesis log
problems.a: Through observation hooks such as VPI callbacks and coverage or assertion monitors
problems.e: Hooks are the observation layer: read state and inject behavior without core changes.

problems.q:
A change request would reorder the Active and NBA regions for speed. Which tier, and what is required?

A) Tier 3, a core edit: it changes LRM semantics and needs human approval and full regression

B) Tier 2: a plug-in

C) Tier 1: a flag

D) No tier: it is harmless
problems.a: Tier 3, a core edit: it changes LRM semantics and needs human approval and full regression
problems.e: Region order is the simulator's correctness contract.

problems.q:
A team wants a custom X-propagation policy that treats X selects on muxes as the merge of both inputs. Where should it go?

A) Tier 1: a seed change

B) In every RTL file

C) Tier 2: a new policy at an X-propagation seam, leaving the core value system untouched

D) Tier 3: rewrite the scheduler
problems.a: Tier 2: a new policy at an X-propagation seam, leaving the core value system untouched
problems.e: A seam with a defined interface lets new X policies plug in without touching the core.

problems.q:
A change request would reorder the Active and NBA regions for speed. Which tier, and what is required?

A) Tier 1: a flag

B) Tier 2: a plug-in

C) No tier: it is harmless

D) Tier 3, a core edit: it changes LRM semantics and needs human approval and full regression
problems.a: Tier 3, a core edit: it changes LRM semantics and needs human approval and full regression
problems.e: Region order is the simulator's correctness contract.

problems.q:
What context must an X-propagation policy seam receive to make its decision?

A) The host CPU type

B) Only the simulation time

C) The waveform file name

D) The operator, the operand values including X bits, and where the operation sits (for example an if condition or a mux select)
problems.a: The operator, the operand values including X bits, and where the operation sits (for example an if condition or a mux select)
problems.e: A policy decides per operation, so it needs the operation and its operands.

problems.q:
What context must an X-propagation policy seam receive to make its decision?

A) The operator, the operand values including X bits, and where the operation sits (for example an if condition or a mux select)

B) Only the simulation time

C) The waveform file name

D) The host CPU type
problems.a: The operator, the operand values including X bits, and where the operation sits (for example an if condition or a mux select)
problems.e: A policy decides per operation, so it needs the operation and its operands.

problems.q:
How should a new scheduling-strategy plug-in be validated before promotion?

A) A compile check only

B) Customer sign-off without tests

C) A single fast benchmark

D) Golden tests and differential runs against the existing simulator on designs that stress ordering and X behavior
problems.a: Golden tests and differential runs against the existing simulator on designs that stress ordering and X behavior
problems.e: Promotion requires the same evidence as any engine change: unchanged results where results should not change.
